title: Runtime Scheduler Testbed and Quality Assurance Manual
author: Priya Kapoor
content:
Overview

This manual describes the runtime scheduler testbed we maintain for validating scheduler policy changes, kernel rollouts, and fidelity-preserving degradation strategies. It documents the architecture of the testbed, the QA workflows, acceptance criteria, regression detection heuristics, and step-by-step procedures to run experiments safely against synthetic and shadow production workloads. The goal is to catch behavioral regressions (latency, fairness, tail-risk), prevent production impact, and provide reproducible evidence for signoff.

Scope

- Kernel and scheduler policy changes (priority changes, preemption rules, admission controller tweaks)
- Scheduler-agent and slot-allocation algorithms
- Admission and backpressure logic (credit accounting, slot reclamation)
- Fidelity/staircase degradation policies and fallback composition
- Telemetry contract validation for scheduler signals

Testbed architecture (high level)

1) Components
- Experiment orchestrator: coordinates scenario provisioning, traffic shaping, and result collection.
- Shadow router: mirrors production request streams into isolated clusters with controlled time offset.
- Synthetic workload generator: produces deterministic mixes for unit tests (see workload catalog below).
- Local kernel harness: runs candidate kernel/scheduler binaries inside container sandboxes with tracer hooks.
- Observability sink: Elasticsearch / Clickhouse for metrics, Jaeger for traces, and artifact store for profiling bundles.

2) Isolation guarantees
- Hardware isolation: testbed uses dedicated GPU pool (label: qa-gpu) to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Network isolation: mirrors run through a VPC peering path with egress-only NAT; no writeback to production control plane.
- Config sandboxing: runtime config is loaded from experiment-specific namespaces; no global flag flips without explicit signoff.

Workload catalog (examples)

- w-small-chat: 95% short prompts (<64 tokens), 5% long (>512 tokens), concurrency 50
- w-bursty-chat: Poisson bursts with 500 rps for 10s every 5m, baseline 20 rps
- w-multi-tenant-mix: 30 tenants, skewed qps distribution, KV cache hit rate target 65%
- w-seq-heavy: long decoding tails, average response 800 tokens, continuous low QPS

Acceptance criteria and QA gates

Run-level acceptance must produce PASS for all checks below before any scheduler change proceeds to staged rollout. Each check has a pass/fail threshold and an owner.

| Check | Metric | Threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Latency SLO | p99 end-to-end generation | <= 1.15x baseline | SRE - Runtime
| Kernel sensitivity | per-kernel 95th percentile op time | <= +15% vs baseline | Runtime Perf
| Fairness | 95th percentile ratio tenant A / tenant median | <= 2.0x | Runtime Ops
| Throughput | sustained tokens/s under nominal load | >= 0.95x baseline | Capacity Planning
| Regression signal | anomaly score (ensemble detector) | < 0.8 (no alarm) | Observability

Note: Baseline is the last released scheduler binary that passed production canary.

QA workflows and procedures

A. Preflight validation (developer)
1. Create an experiment branch and upload candidate scheduler binary to the artifact store.
2. Populate experiment namespace with config: prioritization rules, admission thresholds, and preemption windows. Example YAML: 

apiVersion: v1
kind: SchedulerExperiment
metadata:
  name: qa-priority-test-2025-02
spec:
  admission:
    max_slots_per_tenant: 8
    credit_replenish_ms: 500
  priorities:
    - name: realtime
      weight: 100
    - name: background
      weight: 10

3. Run unit harness: ./tools/sched-harness --binary=artifact://... --workload=w-small-chat --verify-signals
4. Verify trace-level invariants: no kernel preemption loops, no unbounded queue growth.

B. Shadow-validation (engineer + oncall)
1. Schedule a shadow run mirroring a 5% sample of production traffic for 2 hours. Use shadow router config: 
- mirror_ratio: 0.05
- offset: 300s
- bind_to: qa-gpu-pool
2. Monitor the dashboards (links in Observability section).
3. Execute acceptance checks from the table. Block if any check fails.
4. If minor regressions appear (kernel latency increase < 10% but within SLO), tag for controlled canary and schedule remediation experiments.

C. Canary rollout (SRE-led)
1. Canary percentage cadence: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% (min 30m per step and performance stable for 3 consecutive windows).
2. Automated rollback triggers: any of the following -> abort and roll back to baseline.
   - p99 latency > 1.25x baseline for two consecutive windows (5m windows)
   - Kernel error rate increases by >0.5% absolute
   - Unrecoverable fairness violation (tenant starvation detected)
3. Post-canary signoff: runtime product manager + release lead.

Observability and telemetry contract

Minimum telemetry required for any experiment: token-level timing, kernel_id, kernel_phase, scheduler_decision (admit, queue, preempt), tenant_id, queue_depth, slot_allocations. All fields must be present in trace or metric envelopes. Missing fields cause experiment to be rejected.

Suggested dashboards (links are placeholders):
- Scheduler QA Overview: /dashboards/scheduler-qa-overview
- Kernel Heatmap: /dashboards/kernel-heatmap
- Tenant Fairness Matrix: /dashboards/tenant-fairness

Regression detection heuristics

We employ an ensemble of detectors: moving-window z-score, seasonal decomposition residuals, and causal-signal attribution that correlates kernel changes to downstream latencies. Key rules:
- Flag when z-score(p99) > 4 sigma over baseline for 10m
- Correlate kernel_id spikes with p50->p99 divergence using Granger-style causality test (implemented in analysis pipeline)
- Use controlled perturbation runs (see perturbation lab) to map sensitive kernels.

Perturbation lab (controlled experiments)

Purpose: rapidly probe kernel and scheduler behaviour by injecting micro-perturbations and observing knock-on effects. Typical perturbations:
- Small increase in kernel op latency (+5–20%) via CPU throttling per container.
- Forced preemption events every Nth request.
- Synthetic cache misses by clearing kvcache hints.

Procedure:
1. Tag experiment as perturbation-run and ensure artifact retention.
2. Run baseline, then incrementally apply perturbation levels (0%, 5%, 10%, 20%).
3. Collect kernel flamegraphs and trace bundles for each level.
4. Submit a perturbation report (template below) to the experiment tracker.

Perturbation report template (plain text)
- Experiment id: EXP-YYYYMMDD-xxx
- Perturbation type: latency-injection / preemption / cache-eviction
- Affected kernels: kernel_42, kernel_37
- Metrics delta: p50:+3%, p95:+18%, p99:+24%
- Interpretation: kernel_37 has non-linear sensitivity at >10% perturbation; consider moving to fallback kernel variant.

Runbook: Investigate scheduler regression (quick triage)

1. Confirm experiment or production alert: check p50/p95/p99 and kernel error rates.
2. Gather recent artifacts: latest experiment bundle, trace sample, flamegraph, and scheduler decision logs.
3. Reproduce in testbed using the same workload spec. If reproduction fails, escalate to Observability for sampling validation.
4. If reproduced, run bisection: deploy last-known-good scheduler/kernel and progressively switch flags to isolate change.
5. Create incident ticket with severity and owner, schedule rollback if safety thresholds exceeded.

Escalation matrix

- Tier 1 (oncall runtime): initial triage and short-term rollback (first 30 minutes)
- Tier 2 (runtime engineers): in-depth bisection and remediation (30m–4h)
- Tier 3 (product + SRE leadership): customer communication and permanent fixes (>4h)

Operational checklist before any production rollout

- [ ] Experiment artifacts uploaded and retained for 90 days
- [ ] Telemetry contract validated (no missing fields)
- [ ] Synthetic and shadow runs executed with acceptance checks PASS
- [ ] Canary policy pre-configured with rollback hooks
- [ ] Owners and oncall notified with runbook link and signoff list

Appendices

A. CLI recipes
- Launch a local harness: 
  ./tools/sched-harness run --binary artifact://scheduler:v2025-02 --workload w-bursty-chat --collect-traces --out /tmp/exp-bundle
- Submit experiment to orchestrator: 
  curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"experiment":"qa-priority-test-2025-02","binary":"artifact://scheduler:v...","workload":"w-small-chat"}' \
    https://orchestrator.internal/api/v1/experiments

B. Example synthetic workload snippet (YAML)
workload:
  name: w-bursty-chat
  phases:
    - type: steady
      qps: 20
      duration: 2400
    - type: burst
      qps: 500
      duration: 10
      cadence: 300
  token_distribution:
    short: 95
    long: 5

C. Artifact retention and privacy
- All experiment bundles are retained for 90 days in the QA artifact store. Sensitive payloads must be redacted before public sharing. See data-retention policy.

D. Templates and links
- Perturbation report template: /templates/perturbation-report
- Experiment tracker: /tools/experiment-tracker
